title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The 2017 tax cut helped every income group.

Rebuttal: Most households did get some cut in 2018, and that's fair to acknowledge. But the Tax Policy Center estimated the top 1% got an average of about $51,000, middle-income households about $900, and the lowest earners about $40. Everyone got something. The top got almost everything.

Sources: Tax Policy Center, TaxVox, 2018, Tax Policy Center distribution tables, 2017

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Carried interest is a tiny issue that raises almost no money.

Rebuttal: Estimates vary a lot, and some are small. The Tax Foundation put it in the single-digit billions after behavior changes. The JCT estimated about $63 billion over ten years in 2023, and Yale's Budget Lab about $100 billion for a broad version. Even at the low end, it's about fairness. A fund manager's pay is pay, and it should be taxed like a plumber's.

Sources: Joint Committee on Taxation, 2023, CPA Practice Advisor, August 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Most Americans don't pay any taxes, so they have no right to complain about tax policy.

Rebuttal: It's true that a large share of households owe no federal income tax in a given year. But about 80% of households pay payroll taxes, and the Tax Policy Center estimates two in three pay more payroll tax than income tax. Add sales taxes, which in Louisiana run about 10%. Working people pay plenty. They have every right to a say.

Sources: Tax Policy Center estimates, Tax Foundation, State and Local Sales Tax Rates, Midyear 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The payroll tax isn't really a tax because you get Social Security back.

Rebuttal: Social Security does pay benefits back, and it's one of the best programs we have. But the payroll tax still comes out of every paycheck at 7.65%, from the first dollar, with no deductions. It's the biggest federal tax most working families pay. That's a tax, even if it buys something good.

Sources: Social Security Administration, 2026, Tax Policy Center estimates

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Tax breaks aren't spending, so calling them handouts is unfair.

Rebuttal: Technically, a tax break is money not collected rather than money sent out. But the effect on the budget is the same. The Joint Committee on Taxation projects $2.3 trillion in tax expenditures in 2026. The capital gains rate break alone costs $252 billion. If a program of that size went mostly to the wealthy, we'd call it what it is.

Sources: Joint Committee on Taxation, tax expenditure estimates, 2026, CRFB, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The pass-through deduction helps Main Street small businesses.

Rebuttal: Some small business owners do benefit, and they matter. But most of the dollars from the pass-through deduction flow to high-income owners, because that's where the big pass-through profits are. The JCT puts its cost at $76 billion in 2026, and the 2025 law made it permanent. A W-2 worker in the same town gets no 20% deduction.

Sources: Joint Committee on Taxation, tax expenditure estimates, 2026, Tax Policy Center, Briefing Book

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: States that cut income taxes grow faster, so Louisiana did the right thing.

Rebuttal: Some low-tax states have grown fast, and that's a fair observation. But growth depends on many things, like energy, weather, land and population. Louisiana has had low taxes on industry for decades and still ranks high in poverty. ITEP ranked its system the 10th most regressive in the country under 2024 law, even before the flat tax. Low taxes at the top haven't lifted the bottom.

Sources: ITEP, Who Pays? 7th edition, 2024, U.S. Census Bureau, poverty data

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Taxing the rich more would chase them out of Louisiana.

Rebuttal: Some wealthy people do move for taxes, though studies find the effect is smaller than claimed. Louisiana's top 1% already pay about 5.6% of income in state and local taxes after the 2024 changes, ITEP estimated, versus about 13% for the bottom 20%. Asking them to pay closer to what cashiers pay isn't a reason to leave Lafayette for good.

Sources: ITEP analysis of Louisiana tax package, November 2024, ITEP, Who Pays? 7th edition, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana needed to raise the sales tax to balance the budget after cutting income taxes.

Rebuttal: Budgets do have to balance, that's correct. But the state chose to cut income taxes first, at a cost of over $1.1 billion in the first year, then raise the sales tax to cover it. That's a choice to move the burden from the top to the checkout line. It could have balanced the budget by keeping graduated rates or ending industrial exemptions.

Sources: Louisiana Legislative Fiscal Office, reported by Louisiana Illuminator, 2024, ITEP analysis, November 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Repealing the corporate franchise tax makes Louisiana more business friendly.

Rebuttal: Business groups wanted it gone for years, and it's fair to say it was unpopular with them. But in the same package the state raised sales taxes that families pay. Making the state friendly to big business by making it harder on working families isn't a win. Business friendly should include the people who work there.

Sources: Louisiana Illuminator, November 2024, ITEP analysis, November 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Local parish boards still get a say on industrial exemptions.

Rebuttal: They do get a vote, through a single parish board, that's true. But Gov. Landry's 2024 order replaced separate votes by school boards, sheriffs and parishes with one combined vote and kept the governor with final say. It also removed the job creation requirement. A smaller voice with fewer conditions isn't real local control.

Sources: Louisiana Illuminator, February 2024, Good Jobs First, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: ITEP is a left-leaning group, so its numbers can't be trusted.

Rebuttal: ITEP does have a point of view, and readers should know it. But its Who Pays model is used by lawmakers in both parties, and its corporate tax findings come straight from companies' own financial reports. You can check Tesla's tax note yourself. The Tax Foundation, which leans the other way, also ranks Louisiana's sales tax highest in the nation. The facts line up.

Sources: ITEP, April 2026, Tax Foundation, State and Local Sales Tax Rates, Midyear 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The White House billionaire tax study was political spin.

Rebuttal: It came from the Biden White House, and it used a broad definition of income that counts unrealized gains. Critics, including the Tax Foundation, pushed back on that choice, and that's fair to note. But the authors were open about the method, gave a range of 6% to 12%, and every version showed the richest paying less than many top earners on wages. The method is clear. The result holds.

Sources: White House CEA and OMB, 2021, Tax Foundation commentary, 2021

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Corporations pass taxes on to consumers, so taxing them just hurts us.

Rebuttal: Some corporate tax burden does land on workers and consumers, and economists debate how much. But the Treasury, JCT and CBO all assume most of it falls on shareholders and capital owners. When corporations paid less after the 2017 law, ITEP and others found huge buybacks, not lower prices. Taxing corporations still mostly taxes the people who own them.

Sources: Joint Committee on Taxation, distributional methodology, Congressional Budget Office, distribution analyses

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Raising taxes on the rich won't fix Louisiana's problems.

Rebuttal: Taxes alone won't fix everything. Nobody says they will. But the money is real. The 2024 income tax cut costs over $1.1 billion a year. Industrial exemptions have cost parishes more than $20 billion since 1998, by one analysis. That's money for teachers, levees and rural clinics. Fair taxes won't fix everything, but they pay for a lot of fixing.

Sources: Louisiana Legislative Fiscal Office, 2024, Ohio River Valley Institute analysis, cited 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Billionaires are taxed when they die through the estate tax.

Rebuttal: The estate tax does exist, and it can apply to the largest estates. But very few estates pay it, and stepped-up basis erases the income tax on lifetime gains at death. The JCT projects that step-up costs $73 billion in 2026. Wealthy families also use trusts to shrink taxable estates. The fortune grows untaxed for decades. Death isn't a tax event for the gains.

Sources: Joint Committee on Taxation, tax expenditure estimates, 2026, Tax Policy Center, Briefing Book

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Low-income workers get a big refund, so they're not really paying taxes.

Rebuttal: Many do get refunds, often from the EITC and Child Tax Credit, and those credits are real help. But a refund only returns income tax. Payroll tax isn't refunded, at 7.65% from every check. Sales taxes aren't refunded. ITEP found Louisiana's poorest fifth paid 13.1% of income in state and local taxes, more than any other group. The refund doesn't touch that.

Sources: ITEP, Who Pays? 7th edition, 2024, Social Security Administration, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana's EITC already helps poor workers enough.

Rebuttal: Louisiana does have a state EITC, and it helps. But it's 5% of the federal credit, which is small compared with many states. A worker who gets a few dozen dollars back is still paying sales tax at about 10% on everything. A bigger state EITC would be one of the fastest ways to make the system less regressive.

Sources: Louisiana Department of Revenue, ITEP, Who Pays? 7th edition, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Hiring more IRS agents means harassing working families.

Rebuttal: That fear has real roots, because the IRS has leaned on low-income filers. But the cuts didn't stop that. They hit revenue agents, who handle complex returns, harder than anyone, at 31% of early 2025 departures. Cheap letter audits of EITC filers are easy to keep sending. Funding skilled agents is how you shift audits toward the top.

Sources: Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration, 2025, TRAC, Syracuse University, 2023

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Profitable companies that pay zero taxes are using losses from prior years.

Rebuttal: Some companies do carry forward old losses, and that's a legitimate rule. But ITEP's 2025 list specifically excluded companies that zeroed out tax mainly through prior-year losses. The 88 it found paid nothing mostly through breaks like accelerated depreciation, stock options and credits. These were profitable years with zero bills.

Sources: ITEP, April 2026, Thomson Reuters Checkpoint, April 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Corporate tax collections are at record highs, so corporations are paying plenty.

Rebuttal: Total federal revenue was a record $5.3 trillion in fiscal 2025, without adjusting for inflation, as TIGTA noted. But business tax revenue fell 14% that year while individual income tax revenue rose 9%. Workers' share went up. And ITEP found 88 profitable corporations paid nothing at all for 2025.

Sources: Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration, 2026, ITEP, April 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Taxing wealth is un-American.

Rebuttal: Americans have long been wary of new taxes, and that deserves respect. But we already tax wealth. Your house gets a property tax bill every year. In Louisiana, many working families pay property taxes on homes and cars while industrial plants skip 80% of theirs through exemptions. Taxing a billionaire's stock is no stranger than taxing a retiree's house.

Sources: Louisiana Illuminator, February 2024, Tax Policy Center, Briefing Book

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: If you want the rich to pay more, you can pay extra to the IRS yourself.

Rebuttal: Anyone can choose to pay more, that's true. But tax fairness isn't about voluntary gifts. It's about rules that apply to everyone. A worker can't opt out of payroll tax. A billionaire can opt out of income tax by not selling stock. The ask is simple: same rules for wages and wealth.

Sources: White House CEA and OMB, 2021, Joint Committee on Taxation, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: The richest 1% already pay a higher state tax rate because they pay more dollars.

Rebuttal: They do pay more dollars, because they have more income. But a share of income is what matters to a family budget. ITEP found Louisiana's top 1% paid 6.5% of income in state and local taxes under 2024 law, while the poorest fifth paid 13.1%. More dollars, lower rate. The burden falls hardest on those with the least.

Sources: ITEP, Who Pays? 7th edition, 2024, ITEP analysis, November 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Closing loopholes for the rich would hurt retirement savers.

Rebuttal: The largest tax expenditure is the exclusion for retirement savings, $355 billion in 2026, and it helps many workers, though most of the dollars go to higher earners. Nobody is proposing to tax ordinary 401(k)s first. Ending stepped-up basis, taxing carried interest as pay and cutting the capital gains rate gap target fortunes, not a mechanic's IRA.

Sources: Joint Committee on Taxation, tax expenditure estimates, 2026, CRFB, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-counter_argument
author: Claude
text:
Claim: Louisiana's tax cuts will pay for themselves through growth.

Rebuttal: Tax cuts can spur some activity. But the Legislative Fiscal Office estimated the 2024 income tax cut would cost over $1.1 billion in its first budget year, and the state raised the sales tax to cover much of it. Workers pay at the register for a cut that went mostly to the top.

Sources: Louisiana Legislative Fiscal Office, 2024, ITEP, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana's lowest-income 20% paid 13.1% of income in state and local taxes under 2024 law, versus 6.5% for the top 1%

The poorest families in Louisiana paid twice the tax rate of the richest. That's not a rounding error. It's the design. Sales taxes hit every dollar a poor family spends. The rich save and invest, and that money skips the register. Fix the design.

Source: Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, Who Pays? 7th edition, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana had the 10th most regressive state and local tax system in the country under 2024 law

Out of 50 states, only nine had tax systems more tilted against the poor. ITEP found incomes in Louisiana are more unequal after state and local taxes than before. The tax code makes the gap wider. It should close it.

Source: ITEP, Who Pays? 7th edition, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Nationally, the lowest-income 20% paid an average 11.4% of income in state and local taxes in 2024, versus 7.2% for the top 1%

This isn't just a Louisiana problem. Across the country, state and local taxes ask the most of the people with the least. Federal debates get the headlines. State tax codes quietly do the damage.

Source: ITEP, Who Pays? 7th edition, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
ITEP found 44 states' tax systems worsened income inequality in 2024

Forty-four states. Red states and blue states. Most tax systems take a bigger bite from the cashier than the CEO. Tax fairness isn't a party issue. It's a working-class issue.

Source: ITEP, Who Pays? 7th edition, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana's average combined state and local sales tax rate was 10.13% as of July 2026, the highest in the U.S.

Number one in the country, and not in a good way. A sales tax doesn't care if you're buying baby formula or a yacht part. It takes the same cut. For a family that spends everything it earns, that's the biggest tax they pay.

Source: Tax Foundation, State and Local Sales Tax Rates, Midyear 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana raised its state sales tax rate from 4.45% to 5% starting in 2025

The state hiked the tax that hits poor families hardest, right as it cut taxes at the top. The higher rate is set to run through 2029. Every family that shops in Louisiana is paying for that trade.

Source: Louisiana Legislature 2024 special session; Louisiana Illuminator, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana replaced its graduated income tax, which topped out at 4.25%, with a flat 3% rate in 2025

A flat rate sounds fair. But a graduated tax was the one piece of Louisiana's system that asked the rich to pay a little more. Flatten it, and the whole system tilts further toward the bottom.

Source: Louisiana Legislature 2024 special session; Louisiana Illuminator, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana raised its standard deduction to $12,500 for single filers and $25,000 for joint filers in 2025

This part helped working people, and it should be said. But a bigger deduction on income tax can't offset the highest sales tax in the nation. Give with one hand, take at the register with the other.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
ITEP estimated Louisiana's 2024 tax package gave the top 1% an average tax cut of $15,431

The top 1% in Louisiana average about $1.8 million in income, ITEP said. They got $15,431 back. That's a year of rent for a lot of families in Baton Rouge. Relief went where it was needed least.

Source: ITEP analysis of Louisiana tax package, November 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
ITEP estimated middle-income Louisianans got an average tax cut of $87 from the 2024 package

Eighty-seven dollars. That's about a week of groceries before you add the new sales tax. Middle-income families got a coupon. The top got a windfall.

Source: ITEP analysis of Louisiana tax package, November 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
After Louisiana's 2024 tax changes, ITEP estimated the bottom 20% pay about 13% of income in state and local taxes, versus 5.6% for the top 1%

The gap got wider. The top 1% saw their rate drop from 6.5% to 5.6%. The poorest barely moved. That's what 'tax reform' meant in Baton Rouge in 2024.

Source: ITEP analysis of Louisiana tax package, November 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana's Legislative Fiscal Office estimated the 2024 income tax cut would cost over $1.1 billion in its first budget year

A billion dollars a year is real money for a state that ranks near the bottom on health and education. Every dollar given away at the top is a dollar not spent on schools, roads or levees.

Source: Louisiana Legislative Fiscal Office, reported by Louisiana Illuminator, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana's extra sales tax was estimated to raise about $1.1 billion a year

Notice the match. The income tax cut costs about a billion. The sales tax hike raises about a billion. The money didn't vanish. It moved from the top to the checkout line.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, 2024, citing state fiscal estimates

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana cut its top corporate income tax rate from 7.5% to a flat 5.5% starting in 2025

Corporations got a lower rate the same year families got a higher sales tax. Big companies can deduct, defer and shift. A family buying school uniforms can't. Guess who the law was written for.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana repealed its corporate franchise tax for larger businesses in 2024

A tax on corporate capital, gone. Workers didn't get a tax repealed. They got a new sales tax rate. That's the shape of the deal.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Gov. Landry's February 2024 executive order removed the job creation requirement from Louisiana's Industrial Tax Exemption Program

The program lets factories skip 80% of local property taxes. It used to require hiring goals. Now it doesn't. We give up school and sheriff money, and we don't even get a promise of jobs back.

Source: Louisiana Illuminator, February 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Louisiana has awarded more than $20 billion in local industrial property tax breaks since 1998

Twenty billion dollars. That's money parishes could've spent on teachers, deputies and drainage. Instead it stayed with some of the richest companies on earth. That's an estimate, and it's a big one.

Source: Ohio River Valley Institute analysis, reported by Louisiana Illuminator, 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Nine Louisiana LNG export terminals would avoid an estimated $21.1 billion in property taxes through industrial exemptions if all are built

Gas exporters want our coast, our ports and our pipelines. They also want to skip the bill. That works out to about $6.7 million per promised job, by the Sierra Club's estimate. No family gets a deal that sweet.

Source: Sierra Club, The People Always Pay, December 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
One LNG exemption was estimated to cost Plaquemines Parish $834 million from 2025 to 2034, more than double the parish's $62 million total tax revenue in 2023

Plaquemines has lost land, homes and neighbors to storms and the Gulf. Now it stands to lose more than double a year's revenue, every year for a decade. Make the exporter pay its parish.

Source: Sierra Club, The People Always Pay, December 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Plaquemines Parish schools stood to lose an estimated $316 million from one LNG exemption over 2025 to 2034

That's the money for teachers, buses and roofs that don't leak. A gas terminal skips its bill, and kids in Belle Chasse and Port Sulphur pay for it.

Source: Sierra Club, The People Always Pay, December 2024

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The 400 wealthiest U.S. families paid an average federal individual income tax rate of 8.2% from 2010 to 2018, counting unrealized gains as income

An estimate, with a range of 6% to 12%. Even the high end is lower than many working families pay once you add payroll tax. When fortunes grow untaxed, the richest pay less than the people who serve them coffee.

Source: White House Council of Economic Advisers and Office of Management and Budget, 2021

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Tax expenditures in the federal tax code are projected to total $2.3 trillion in 2026

That's spending through the tax code, and it's bigger than a lot of federal programs combined. Some of it helps working families. Much of it flows to people who already have the most.

Source: Joint Committee on Taxation, tax expenditure estimates, reported by CRFB, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Lower tax rates on capital gains and dividends are projected to cost $252 billion in 2026

The second biggest tax break in the code goes to income from owning, not working. A quarter of a trillion dollars a year. Imagine that money in child care and rural hospitals.

Source: Joint Committee on Taxation, reported by CRFB, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Stepped-up basis on assets passed at death is projected to cost $73 billion in 2026

When a rich person dies, the tax on a lifetime of gains disappears. Heirs start fresh. That's the 'die' in buy, borrow, die. Seventy-three billion dollars a year, gone.

Source: Joint Committee on Taxation, reported by CRFB, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The pass-through business income deduction is projected to cost $76 billion in 2026

Many business owners can deduct up to 20% of qualified income. Wage workers can't deduct 20% of a paycheck. The 2025 law made this break permanent.

Source: Joint Committee on Taxation, reported by CRFB, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The ten largest federal tax expenditures together exceed $1.4 trillion in 2026

The tax code is a budget too. Where the breaks go tells you who has lobbyists. Some help workers. The biggest checks go up the ladder.

Source: Joint Committee on Taxation, reported by CRFB, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The top federal tax rate on long-term capital gains is 20%, plus a 3.8% net investment income tax, versus 37% on top wages in 2026

Same dollar, different rules. Earn it with your hands and the top rate is 37%. Earn it from stock and it's 23.8% at most. That gap is a choice Congress makes, and it can unmake it.

Source: Internal Revenue Code; IRS, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Workers pay 7.65% of wages in Social Security and Medicare taxes, matched by employers, for a combined 15.3%

No deductions. No loopholes. The payroll tax starts on the first dollar of every paycheck. Workers fund Social Security and Medicare every week. Don't let anyone tell you they don't pay taxes.

Source: Social Security Administration; IRS, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
About two in three U.S. households pay more in payroll taxes than in federal income taxes

The income tax gets all the attention. For most working families, the payroll tax is the bigger bite. That's an estimate, but the pattern has held for years. Look at a pay stub.

Source: Tax Policy Center estimate, 2013 projection for 2023

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The Joint Committee on Taxation estimated in 2023 that taxing carried interest as ordinary income would raise about $63 billion over ten years

Estimates range widely, from a few billion to around $100 billion, because carried interest isn't reported on its own line. The principle doesn't change. A fund manager's pay should be taxed like a welder's.

Source: Joint Committee on Taxation, 2023, reported by CPA Practice Advisor, 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
At least 88 large, profitable U.S. corporations paid $0 in federal income tax for 2025

Eighty-eight companies, many of them household names. Profits on the books, zero on the tax bill. ITEP calls the list far from complete. Every worker on their payroll paid more.

Source: Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, April 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The 88 zero-tax corporations reported more than $105 billion in combined U.S. pretax income for 2025

Over $105 billion in profit and not a dime of federal income tax. At the 21% legal rate, that's a $26.7 billion tax break in one year, ITEP said.

Source: ITEP, April 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
The 88 zero-tax corporations received $4.7 billion in federal income tax rebates for 2025

Not just zero. Below zero. Profitable companies got money back from the Treasury. If a worker tried that, the IRS would send a letter. These companies got a check.

Source: ITEP, April 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Tesla paid no federal income tax on almost $5.7 billion of U.S. income in 2025

One of the most valuable companies on earth. Billions in U.S. profit. A federal income tax bill of zero. Meanwhile, its line workers paid tax on every hour.

Source: ITEP, April 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
United Airlines paid no federal income tax on almost $4.3 billion of U.S. income in 2025

Flight attendants and baggage handlers paid their taxes. The airline paid none on billions in profit. That's the system working exactly as written. Rewrite it.

Source: ITEP, April 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Tesla paid federal income taxes equal to 4.9% of $315 billion in combined U.S. profits in 2025

Four tech giants avoided about $51 billion compared with the 21% legal rate, ITEP estimated. Their profits rose by about a third. Their tax rate fell to a sliver. Workers paid more than that out of their first paycheck.

Source: ITEP, February 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Accelerated depreciation reduced the 88 zero-tax corporations' 2025 federal taxes by $11.4 billion

Write off a machine faster than it wears out, and your tax bill shrinks today. The 2025 federal law made full expensing permanent. Workers can't depreciate their trucks that fast.

Source: ITEP, April 2026

title: Claude Drop: taxes-data_narrative
author: Claude
text:
Chevron, ConocoPhillips and Exxon paid an average effective federal tax rate of about 6% on roughly $23 billion in 2025 U.S. profits

Louisiana gives the oil industry its coast and its parish tax base. The industry gives Washington about 6 cents on the profit dollar. Workers in Lake Charles pay more than that in payroll tax alone.

Source: FACT Coalition analysis, reported by Thomson Reuters, April 2026
